title: I Made the Open Mic Host Keep His Own Five-Minute Rule

parts.text: I started the set timer when the host went six minutes over, again. I am twenty-six, designer by day, jokes at night. The host, Rex, had a five-minute rule he printed on the chalkboard. Chalk dust sat on the bar like snow. Rex's friends always got extra. My friend Noor held the cheap kitchen timer we brought. The beer taps hissed. Rex said, "Don't police the art" I said, "Your chalkboard already did" Rex pointed at me. He hated being timed. I can still name the ugly little detail, which is how I know it happened. I noticed a scuff on the floor shaped like a comma, which fit i. Someone had left a receipt in the cup holder, faded blue ink. The air tasted like leftover rain and cleaning spray, which fit i. A cheap clock on the wall jumped a minute late, then caught up. I kept my keys in my left pocket so I would not fidget, which fit i. The plastic chair stuck to my legs when I shifted. A vending machine hummed in another room like a bored insect, which fit i. I counted three ceiling tiles with water stains before I spoke again. My socks had a hole I had been ignoring since Tuesday, which fit i.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The kitchen timer is ringing on his sixth minute, and the chalkboard still says five.

parts.text: The timer rang. The room laughed at the object, not at me. Rex called me a cop. The bartender, Sal, who actually owns the nights, took the mic. He said five means five, including Rex. I did my five, clean. Rex's friends heckled on a delay. Sal cut the mics. The chalkboard got a second line: HOST TOO. I still go. I still bring the timer because theater is logistics. Rex does four now, which is growth. Chalk dust still gets on my sleeves. I accept it. Sal said, "Five includes you" Rex said, "This is a witch hunt" Noor kept the timer.
